title: Parallel Inheritance Hierarchies (Parallel Type Implementations)
pattern: For every new type added in one domain hierarchy, a developer is forced to write a corresponding type implementation in a parallel hierarchy, typically sharing matching prefixes or suffixes (e.g., `ActiveDeal` and `TabularActiveStyle`).
why_bad: It tightly couples independent dimensions of variation. Extending the system with a new variant requires duplicate work and matching structural configuration in two separate files. If a developer implements a new `Deal` type but forgets to create its matching `PresentationStyle`, a runtime error or structural gap occurs.
detection: Two or more distinct traits or enum groupings in separate modules where the list of concrete implementers/variants matches 1:1, especially if their type names share identical prefixes or suffixes.
counterexample: Standard implementations of universal traits (like `std::fmt::Display` or `serde::Serialize`) where the type system naturally requires separate formatting or serialization behavior for every concrete type.
fix: Merge the parallel hierarchies using delegation. Let the primary class hold a reference to a single generic strategy style or use a single multi-dimensional mapper instead of duplicated class trees.
source: Martin Fowler, *Refactoring*, Chapter 3 ("Parallel Inheritance Hierarchies"); Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Chapter 24 ("Inheritance hierarchies have to be modified in parallel"), pp. 212, 570.
